To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

unsupervised visual learning of complex stimuli improves the accuracy of the judgments, reduces the errors with both different and same pairs, and increases the bias for different response, which can be attributed to a stimulus processing bias.

1) the same‐different discrimination learning is an unsupervised process that increases the sensitivity and reduces the errors with both types of stimuli pairs, 2) with practice, the discrimination performance improves for different pairs and there is a bias to respond “different”, 3) the bias for different response is a stimulus processing bias that is modulated by the proportion of same pairs, 4) the acquired discrimination is transferred to novel exemplar of the practiced stimuli.

unsupervised visual complex stimulus discrimination learning is characterized by an increase in the sensory evidence and a decrease in the response criterion, which results in an improvement in the sensitivity, and the development of a stimulus processing bias that favors different responses.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanisms that allow the human visual system to discriminate a variety of stimuli and how this ability is shaped by unsupervised learning.
the mechanisms underlying the same‐different judgment, which has been largely neglected, and provides new insights on how learning shapes the discrimination of unfamiliar complex stimuli.
the mechanisms of visual discrimination learning and the role of perceptual learning in category specific perceptual learning.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the discrimination learning is based on the improvement of the sensory evidence and the precision of the sensory memory.

visual discrimination learning occurs in the absence of labels or individuation, and that it improves the sensory evidence and the working memory precision of the stimuli, leading to a perceptual expertise that is fully transferred to novel stimuli.
visual learning is a complex process involving a variety of factors and mechanisms that need further investigation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have shown that the same‐different discrimination is a process of learning that improves with practice, and it is based on the acquisition of category specific perceptual representations that are fully generalizable to new exemplars of the trained stimuli.
the same‐different discrimination is a fundamental ability that improves through unsupervised learning, and this process is based on changes in the processing of sensory information.

unsupervised visual learning of complex stimuli occurs in the absence of individuation and is based on changes in the stimulus encoding and processing that increase sensory evidence and/or working memory precision.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the same‐different discrimination of complex stimuli is a flexible and robust learning process.
the same‐different discrimination of complex stimuli can be improved by learning in the absence of explicit feedback, with an increased sensitivity and a bias for the different response.
unsupervised learning of same‐different judgments can be used to improve discrimination of complex visual stimuli.
